newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada to look into new charges country a Nazi haven.
newsitem.headline: Canada to look into new charges country a Nazi haven.

text.p: A Jewish group accused Canada on Tuesday of being one of the world's "safest havens" for Nazi war criminals after a claim that 157 former Nazis were living in the country.
A report in the Jerusalem Post over the weekend said an American private investigator uncovered a slew of alleged Nazis living comfortably in Canada without any fear of prosecution.

Canadian Justice Minister Allan Rock said on Monday he was ready to investigate the new charges, although he doubted so many Nazi war criminals could still be living in Canada. He said Canada's efforts over the past 10 years should have reduced the number in the country.
But Bernie Farber, national director of community relations for the Canadian Jewish Congress in Toronto, said he was not surprised by the report.
"Canada has become one of the safest havens in the world for Nazi war criminals," Farber said. "We've known for years that these people have walked among us freely."

The Jerusalem Post report said Steve Rambam, of New York, posed as a university student and talked to suspected Nazi war criminals in Canada while pretending to do research on law enforcement during the Second World War.

"Although Austria or Argentina would seem more fertile ground for Nazi hunting, Canada's expansive, multi-ethnic society -- and Ottawa's long-time indifference to Nazis -- has provided a near-blissful refuge for war criminals," the report stated.
The report said Rambam taped many of his conversations and some spoke freely of their past.

"When speaking to Rambam, few of the alleged Nazi war criminals, of course, came out openly and admitted to personally persecuting the Jews. But most acknowledged they were members of notorious units which collaborated actively with the Nazis and which in many countries would constitute grounds for deportation," the article stated.

Canada has failed to convict any suspected Nazi war criminals under a 1987 law that allows it to prosecute people for crimes that would have broken Canadian law when committed in other countries during wartime.
The cases have been extremely difficult to complete, since many of the witnesses were too old or sick to testify.
Canada announced in 1995 it would try a new tact of using immigration procedures to deport suspected Nazi criminals but has run into a number of legal snags.

Jewish groups have long complained that thousands of Nazi war criminals entered Canada after the war and the problem was ignored by the federal government during the country's preoccupation with the Cold War and other problems. It was not until the mid 1980s that a made a concerted effort to track down alleged criminals involved in the Jewish Holocaust.
